narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 60.5% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is a risk estimate, not a certainty: it placed you slightly above the school’s concern threshold, and the law school used that prediction as the reason to reject admission.

The strongest factor was your year-three grade standing: you were in the first decile, while admitted students averaged around the sixth decile, and this pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. The second most influential factor was your LSAT score. At 33.50 it is below the admitted-student average of about 37.18, but in this prediction it was the only top factor that pushed toward passing; it was not enough to offset the other signals. The third factor was your year-one standing, also first decile versus an admitted average near the sixth, and it again pushed toward failure. Your gender and race were not used in the prediction.

To move forward, ask admissions whether there is an appeal or reconsideration process and what additional evidence would help. Consider retaking the LSAT after structured preparation, strengthening your academic record, and presenting a concrete bar-exam readiness plan. An admissions advisor can clarify whether a later application or conditional pathway is realistic.
